newsitem.title: FRANCE: French PM raps Socialists, rightists start poll bid.
newsitem.headline: French PM raps Socialists, rightists start poll bid.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe derided the Socialist opposition's growth-boosting policies on Thursday as the far-right National Front launched its own campaign with a virulent attack on President Jacques Chirac.

The Gaullist prime minister told a party conference that voters must choose in May-June parliamentary elections between lasting economic growth with his centre-right government and an "artificial boost" with the Socialists.

They had a choice between "a society in which people participate and a society where regulation rules." The opposition Socialists have said they would seek to stimulate consumer demand to engineer faster growth.

Juppe's audience included only a few of the heavyweights in his fractious bloc, including ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur. Both National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin and ex-interior minister Charles Pasqua, outspoken Juppe critics, stayed away.

"The Socialists want to eradicate unemployment by creating jobs with decrees. They regulate from above...We need to rebuild the confidence of the new generations in employment," said Juppe, his popularity down as unemployment has risen from 11.7 percent when he took office in 1995 to a record 12.8 percent.

Balladur and Education Minister Francois Bayrou sounded radically different tones on the free market. "Liberalism liberates no one," Bayrou said to cheers. A few minutes later, Balladur called for "liberalism as a condition of progress".

At a May Day parade through Paris of some 9,000 supporters, far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen and the National Front launched his drive for a toehold in parliament with a vitriolic attack on European union, immigrants and Chirac.
He accused Chirac and the government of ignoring immigration and high unemployment while seeking to jettison the national identity, and he urged voters to "throw them out" of office.

"You (Chirac) have always betrayed your friends, your ideas, your campaign promises, and today you are asking for a blank cheque to betray France by submerging it in the Europe of Maastricht," Le Pen said.

Le Pen's traditional May Day festival, honouring mediaeval heroine Joan of Arc who drove the English out of France, was broadened this year to advance the Front's bid for seats in the National Assembly, where it currently has none.

The Front, which wants to ship immigrants home and give a constitutional preference to "native-born French" in jobs and social benefits, has set a goal of 20 seats in parliamentary elections. Pollsters predict it will win a handful at most.

Le Pen, who announced on the eve of the parade that he would not himself run in the election, has targeted the centre-right, saying the Front's priority was to "zap" it from power even if it meant a victory for the left.

Police said the march went off without incident but a member of the royalist Action Francaise was injured when members of the Betar Jewish youth movement stopped a mass in memory of World War Two collaborationist leader Marshal Philippe Petain.
Several of France's main trade union leaders, divided on cuts in working hours and other employment issues, bowed out of a leftist May Day union rally in Paris.

Marc Blondel, leader of the non-partisan Force Ouvriere, staged a rally in Bordeaux, in southwest France, where Juppe is mayor, and told reporters: "I don't want to give public opinion the idea that we are all agreed".
